messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Product Manager
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 55

# Clinical Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A is a 58-year-old South Asian man who presents with a haunted quality that he cannot quite name. He arrives for each session precisely on time, carrying a leather messenger bag that he keeps clutched in his lap throughout the hour. His hands seldom rest—they grip the bag strap, smooth his tie, tap against his thigh. He smiles often, but the smile never reaches his eyes; it is a practiced social reflex, a mask he learned to wear long before the trauma.

The story he tells begins not in the present, but twenty-two years ago, in the country where he was born and raised. Mr. A was a civil engineer then, working for a government contractor. During a period of political instability, he was detained for questioning about a colleague’s alleged opposition activities. The questioning lasted five days. He describes it in fragments: the windowless room, the smell of sweat and diesel, the men who did not give their names. They used electric shocks on his hands and feet, beat the soles with rubber hoses, and suspended him by his wrists for hours. On the third day, they forced him to sign a confession he could not read. He was released without charges, but the country was no longer safe for him. Within a month, he and his wife fled to Canada with two suitcases and a three-year-old daughter.

Now, twenty-two years later, Mr. A is a product manager at a mid-sized software firm. From the outside, he is successful: he leads a team of twelve, delivers quarterly reviews, and has never missed a deadline. But inside the office, he is a man perpetually bracing for interrogation. When his manager calls a last-minute meeting, his heart slams against his ribs. He hears the words “we need to talk” and his mind instantly goes to the windowless room. He has learned to hide this—he excuses himself to the bathroom, splashes cold water on his face, and repeats a silent mantra: *You are safe. You are in Canada. No one is coming.* But the physical response does not listen. His hands shake. His stomach clenches. He avoids eye contact with senior leadership because looking at a man in a suit triggers the old smell of diesel.

At home, the trauma lives in the spaces between words. His wife, Amrita, has grown used to his startle response—a sudden knock on the door, the buzz of the intercom, the unexpected touch on the shoulder from behind. He has not slept through the night in years. Most nights, he wakes at 3:00 a.m., convinced he hears footsteps in the hallway. He checks the locks three times before bed. He never sits with his back to a door in a restaurant. His daughter, now 25, once asked him why he flinched when she hugged him from behind. He said he was “just tired.” He cannot bring himself to tell her what happened. The shame is a living thing inside him—the shame of being weak, of signing that confession, of running away.

His PCL-5 score of 55 reflects what he will not say aloud: intrusive images of the rubber hose, nightmares of being suspended, a constant sense of a foreshortened future. He has not returned to his home country, not even for his mother’s funeral three years ago. He told his family it was too expensive. The truth is that the thought of an airport, of a uniformed official, of a passport check, fills him with a dread that borders on paralysis.

He comes to therapy because his wife threatened to leave. Not out of anger, she said, but out of loneliness. She cannot reach him. He knows this. He wants to be reached. But every time he tries to speak the words—*the room, the wires, the men*—his throat closes. So he sits in the chair, bag on his lap, and he tells me about product roadmaps and sprint cycles, and he waits for the hour to end.
